claim: Distinct microbial ecosystems have evolved to meet the challenges of indoor environments.
source: Distinct microbial ecosystems have evolved to meet the challenges of indoor environments, shaping the microbial communities that interact most with modern human activities.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Microbial transmission in food-processing facilities has an enormous impact on the qualities and healthfulness of foods.
source: Microbial transmission in food-processing facilities has an enormous impact on the qualities and healthfulness of foods, beneficially or detrimentally interacting with food products.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of microbial transmission in food processing, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The study profiled hop-resistance gene frequencies and bacterial and fungal communities in a brewery.
source: To explore modes of microbial transmission and spoilage-gene frequency in a commercial food-production scenario, we profiled hop-resistance gene frequencies and bacterial and fungal communities in a brewery.
evidence: This describes the methods and data collection performed in the study.

claim: A Bayesian approach was employed for predicting routes of contamination.
source: We employed a Bayesian approach for predicting routes of contamination, revealing critical control points for microbial management.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: Physically mapping microbial populations over time illustrates patterns of dispersal and identifies potential contaminant reservoirs within the brewery environment.
source: Physically mapping microbial populations over time illustrates patterns of dispersal and identifies potential contaminant reservoirs within this environment.
evidence: This describes findings from the spatial and temporal analysis performed in the study.

claim: Habitual exposure to beer is associated with increased abundance of spoilage genes.
source: Habitual exposure to beer is associated with increased abundance of spoilage genes, predicting greater contamination risk.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings on spoilage gene distribution.

claim: Building materials, substrates, and physiochemical conditions encountered by microbes in food-processing facilities differ dramatically from outdoor conditions.
source: Like other indoor environments, the building materials, substrates, and physiochemical conditions encountered by microbes in food-processing facilities differ dramatically from the outdoor conditions to which microbial life evolved (Kelley and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kelley and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: The microbial communities of homes, office buildings, and hospitals can influence the health of their inhabitants.
source: While the microbial communities of other indoor environments, such as homes (Lax et al., 2014), office buildings (Kembel et al., 2014), and hospitals (Bokulich et al., 2013a), can influence the health of their inhabitants, food-production facilities represent a unique type of built environment wherein microbial activities are intimately tied to product-quality outcomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on homes, office buildings, and hospitals.

claim: Food-production facilities represent a unique type of built environment wherein microbial activities are intimately tied to product-quality outcomes.
source: While the microbial communities of other indoor environments, such as homes (Lax et al., 2014), office buildings (Kembel et al., 2014), and hospitals (Bokulich et al., 2013a), can influence the health of their inhabitants, food-production facilities represent a unique type of built environment wherein microbial activities are intimately tied to product-quality outcomes.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing on knowledge of different built environments.

claim: Both beneficial and detrimental microbial activities are well defined in foods.
source: Furthermore, both beneficial and detrimental microbial activities are well defined in foods, making these systems a useful model for exploring microbial ecosystem dynamics beyond the scope of contaminant mitigation.
evidence: This draws on established knowledge in food microbiology.

claim: Microbial activity is central to the production of fermented foods including beer.
source: Fermented foods, including beer, have the additional distinction that microbial activity is central to their production, responsible for necessary transformations as well as product spoilage (Bokulich et al., 2012a; Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most modern food-fermentation practices occur under relatively aseptic conditions, employing pure starter cultures.
source: Most modern food-fermentation practices occur under relatively aseptic conditions, employing pure starter cultures in their production, and environmental contamination represents a prevalent threat to product integrity (Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and draws on knowledge of modern fermentation practices.

claim: Beer is typically produced through fermentation of malted barley sugars (wort) to alcohol by pure strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae or Saccharomyces pastorianus.
source: Beer is typically produced through fermentation of malted barley sugars (wort) to alcohol by pure strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae or Saccharomyces pastorianus, and any additional organisms—including cross-contamination from different Saccharomyces strains used in the same facility—are considered contaminants (Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This describes standard beer production practices and is supported by a citation.

claim: Any additional organisms in beer production, including cross-contamination from different Saccharomyces strains, are considered contaminants.
source: Beer is typically produced through fermentation of malted barley sugars (wort) to alcohol by pure strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae or Saccharomyces pastorianus, and any additional organisms—including cross-contamination from different Saccharomyces strains used in the same facility—are considered contaminants (Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013.

claim: In coolship beer production, no starter cultures are added to the wort.
source: For example, in the production of coolship (lambic-style) beers, a type of sour beer, no starter cultures are added to the wort; instead, boiled wort is allowed to cool overnight in a shallow, open-top vessel known as a coolship where indigenous microbiota are presumably introduced to the product, initiating fermentation (Van Oevelen et al., 1977; Bokulich et al., 2012b; Spitaels et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the coolship beer production process and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In coolship beer production, boiled wort is allowed to cool overnight in a shallow, open-top vessel where indigenous microbiota are presumably introduced to the product.
source: For example, in the production of coolship (lambic-style) beers, a type of sour beer, no starter cultures are added to the wort; instead, boiled wort is allowed to cool overnight in a shallow, open-top vessel known as a coolship where indigenous microbiota are presumably introduced to the product, initiating fermentation (Van Oevelen et al., 1977; Bokulich et al., 2012b; Spitaels et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the coolship process and is supported by citations.

claim: The unique succession of indigenous microbiota in coolship ale fermentations sets them apart chemically and sensorially from other beers.
source: The unique succession of indigenous microbiota in coolship ale fermentations sets them apart chemically and sensorially from other beers (Van Oevelen et al., 1976; Spaepen et al., 1978), making coolship breweries a particularly interesting system for tracking microbial populations in food-processing environments.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Van Oevelen et al., 1976 and Spaepen et al., 1978.

claim: Beer is protected from wholesale microbial contamination through its alcoholic, low-pH, and antimicrobial properties.
source: Beer is protected from wholesale microbial contamination through its alcoholic, low-pH, and antimicrobial properties, and modern sanitary technologies and practices minimize the threat of spoilage organisms that have evolved specifically to grow in beer (Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This describes the antimicrobial properties of beer and is supported by a citation.

claim: Biofilms and other environmental reservoirs remain potential sources of microbial contamination in breweries.
source: Nevertheless, biofilms and other environmental reservoirs remain potential sources of microbial contamination in breweries (Timke et al., 2005; Storgards et al., 2006; Timke et al., 2008; Mamvura et al., 2011; Matoulkova et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on biofilms in breweries.

claim: As wort is boiled prior to fermentation, the primary reservoir for spoilage microorganisms in beer production is the brewery environment.
source: As wort is boiled prior to fermentation, the primary reservoir for spoilage microorganisms in beer production is the brewery environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the brewing process where boiling sterilizes the wort.

claim: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are of particular concern in beer production as some members resist hop antimicrobial compounds.
source: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are of particular concern, as some members of this clade resist hop antimicrobial compounds, enabling growth and spoilage of beer through acidification, hazes, and off-flavors (Suzuki et al., 2006; Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2006 and Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013.

claim: Hop iso-alpha-acids kill most Gram-positive bacteria by acting as ionophores, dissipating proton-motive force across cell walls.
source: Hop iso-alpha-acids, the primary antimicrobial compounds in beer, kill most Gram-positive bacteria by acting as ionophores, dissipating proton-motive force across cell walls (Simpson and Fernandez, 1992, 1994; Simpson, 1993a), and via oxidative stress (Behr and Vogel, 2010).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to Simpson and Fernandez, 1992, 1994; Simpson, 1993a; and Behr and Vogel, 2010.

claim: Hop iso-alpha-acids kill bacteria via oxidative stress.
source: Hop iso-alpha-acids, the primary antimicrobial compounds in beer, kill most Gram-positive bacteria by acting as ionophores, dissipating proton-motive force across cell walls (Simpson and Fernandez, 1992, 1994; Simpson, 1993a), and via oxidative stress (Behr and Vogel, 2010).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to Behr and Vogel, 2010.

claim: The multi-drug transporters horA and horC are hop-resistance mechanisms.
source: Very few resistance mechanisms have been proposed (Suzuki et al., 2006), primarily being the multi-drug transporters horA (Sami et al., 1997; Sakamoto et al., 2001) and horC (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), the transcriptional regulator of horC, horB (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), and hitA, a divalent cation transporter (Hayashi et al., 2001) that imports manganese into the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies identifying these genes.

claim: horB is the transcriptional regulator of horC.
source: Very few resistance mechanisms have been proposed (Suzuki et al., 2006), primarily being the multi-drug transporters horA (Sami et al., 1997; Sakamoto et al., 2001) and horC (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), the transcriptional regulator of horC, horB (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), and hitA, a divalent cation transporter (Hayashi et al., 2001) that imports manganese into the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2005 and Iijima et al., 2006.

claim: hitA is a divalent cation transporter that imports manganese into the cell.
source: Very few resistance mechanisms have been proposed (Suzuki et al., 2006), primarily being the multi-drug transporters horA (Sami et al., 1997; Sakamoto et al., 2001) and horC (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), the transcriptional regulator of horC, horB (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), and hitA, a divalent cation transporter (Hayashi et al., 2001) that imports manganese into the cell.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayashi et al., 2001.

claim: Hop-resistance genes are all located on plasmids and transmit via horizontal gene transfer.
source: These genes are all located on plasmids and transmit via horizontal gene transfer (Suzuki et al., 2005, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2005, 2006.

claim: A total of 501 samples were collected during three seasons from the brewery.
source: A total of 501 samples were collected during three seasons, representing the main processing surfaces and equipment used throughout the brewing process (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the sample collection performed in the study.

claim: Many samples cluster by processing room and substrate type regardless of season based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity.
source: Bray–Curtis dissimilarity of complete microbial profiles reveals that many samples cluster by processing room and substrate type regardless of season (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the beta-diversity analysis shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: Fermenter samples cluster and are associated with Bacillaceae.
source: Thus, fermenter samples cluster, associated with Bacillaceae; cellar production areas, associated with Micrococcaceae (including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus); wort, malt, and hotside (wort-preparation) surfaces, associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula; barrel-room floor samples, associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae; and beer samples, associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Cellar production areas are associated with Micrococcaceae including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus.
source: Thus, fermenter samples cluster, associated with Bacillaceae; cellar production areas, associated with Micrococcaceae (including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus); wort, malt, and hotside (wort-preparation) surfaces, associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula; barrel-room floor samples, associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae; and beer samples, associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Wort, malt, and hotside surfaces are associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula.
source: Thus, fermenter samples cluster, associated with Bacillaceae; cellar production areas, associated with Micrococcaceae (including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus); wort, malt, and hotside (wort-preparation) surfaces, associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula; barrel-room floor samples, associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae; and beer samples, associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Barrel-room floor samples are associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae.
source: Thus, fermenter samples cluster, associated with Bacillaceae; cellar production areas, associated with Micrococcaceae (including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus); wort, malt, and hotside (wort-preparation) surfaces, associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula; barrel-room floor samples, associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae; and beer samples, associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Beer samples are associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Thus, fermenter samples cluster, associated with Bacillaceae; cellar production areas, associated with Micrococcaceae (including the beer-spoiling genera Kocuria and Micrococcus); wort, malt, and hotside (wort-preparation) surfaces, associated with Enterobacteriaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Candida santamariae, Pichia, and Rhodotorula; barrel-room floor samples, associated with Staphylococcaceae and Carnobacteriaceae; and beer samples, associated with Lactobacillaceae and Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Barrels cluster and are associated with Aspergillus, Eurotium, and Penicillium.
source: Barrels cluster, associated with Aspergillus, Eurotium, and Penicillium; coolship and barrel-room samples with Cryptococcus and Cladosporium.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: Coolship and barrel-room samples are associated with Cryptococcus and Cladosporium.
source: Barrels cluster, associated with Aspergillus, Eurotium, and Penicillium; coolship and barrel-room samples with Cryptococcus and Cladosporium.
evidence: This describes clustering patterns observed in the data analysis.

claim: The taxonomic trends demonstrate significant site associations (Kruskal–Wallis Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.05).
source: These taxonomic trends each demonstrate significant site associations (Kruskal–Wallis Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.05).
evidence: This reports the statistical significance of the observed associations.

claim: S. cerevisiae was common throughout the brewery, but especially in the fermentation cellar.
source: S. cerevisiae was common throughout the brewery, but especially in the fermentation cellar.
evidence: This describes the distribution of S. cerevisiae observed in the study.

claim: LAB and acetic acid bacteria were found sporadically at different sites and times, including on and near packaging equipment and fermenters inoculated with LAB.
source: LAB and acetic acid bacteria were found sporadically at different sites and times, including on and near packaging equipment and fermenters inoculated with LAB (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the distribution of LAB and acetic acid bacteria observed in the study, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Grains were predicted as the largest microbial contributor to hotside areas, almost all surfaces in the coolship room, and areas of the cellar away from the main fermentation area.
source: Grains were predicted as the largest microbial contributor to hotside areas, almost all surfaces in the coolship room, and areas of the cellar away from the main fermentation area.
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Hops were predicted as the major contributor to cellar fermentation areas and fermentation equipment.
source: Hops were predicted as the major contributor to cellar fermentation areas and fermentation equipment.
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Yeast was predicted as the highest contributor to fermenters, conditioning tanks, and packaging equipment.
source: Yeast was predicted as the highest contributor to fermenters, conditioning tanks, and packaging equipment.
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Beer was predicted to be a common contaminant around fermenters and barrels within the cellar.
source: Beer was predicted to be a common contaminant around fermenters and barrels within the cellar.
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Skin was a minor contributor to some surfaces in the cellar.
source: Skin was a minor contributor to some surfaces in the cellar.
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Outdoor air, soil, saliva, feces, freshwater, and ocean water were predicted to provide only a very low level of contamination (<0.001 relative abundance).
source: Outdoor air, soil, saliva, feces, freshwater, and ocean water were predicted to provide only a very low level of contamination (<0.001 relative abundance).
evidence: This is a result from the SourceTracker analysis predicting contamination sources.

claim: Raw substrates are the main contaminant sources within the brewery, compared to extraneous sources.
source: These results suggest that raw substrates are the main contaminant sources within the brewery, compared to extraneous sources.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SourceTracker analysis results.

claim: Substrate contact drives the microbial communities of different brewery surfaces.
source: These findings suggest that substrate contact drives the microbial communities of different brewery surfaces.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering and source-tracking analyses.

claim: Raw materials (grain, hops, yeast) may be important vectors for any spoilage organisms encountered in the facility.
source: Consequently, raw materials (grain, hops, yeast) may be important vectors for any spoilage organisms encountered in the facility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that substrate contact drives microbial communities.

claim: Substrate-centric community structuring has been observed in other food facilities.
source: This substrate-centric community structuring has also been observed in other food facilities (Bokulich and Mills, 2013a; Bokulich et al., 2013b, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in other food facilities.

claim: The brewery surface niches clustered throughout time with only subtle changes across seasons, unlike wineries which were significantly impacted by seasonal factors.
source: However, the brewery surface niches clustered throughout time with only subtle changes across seasons, unlike wineries, which were significantly impacted by seasonal factors (Bokulich et al., 2013b).
evidence: This compares the findings of this study to a previous study on wineries, supported by a citation.

claim: Beer production is a continual year-round process, creating a stable environment on equipment surfaces.
source: The raw materials for beer are stored and processed throughout the year in a continual production schedule, creating a stable environment on equipment surfaces that interact with these same raw substrates on a daily basis.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed stability of microbial communities over time.

claim: Brewery environments may function like cheese-making environments, where facility-specific 'house' microbial communities form on equipment surfaces.
source: Instead, brewery environments may function more like cheese-making environments, where facility-specific 'house' microbial communities form on equipment surfaces in response to idiosyncrasies in the indoor environment (Bokulich and Mills, 2013a).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison supported by a citation to a study on cheese-making environments.

claim: S. cerevisiae progressed from dominating fermentation and packaging areas only in Autumn to being the most abundant fungus detected across the brewery in Spring and Summer.
source: Several populations visibly spread with time, most prominently S. cerevisiae, which progressed from dominating fermentation and packaging areas only in Autumn to being the most abundant fungus detected across the brewery in Spring and Summer.
evidence: This describes temporal changes in S. cerevisiae distribution observed in the spatial mapping data.

claim: C. santamariae displayed high abundance on hotside surfaces in Autumn but became more abundant and spread to nearby sections of the cellar in Spring and Summer.
source: Likewise, C. santamariae displayed high abundance on hotside surfaces in Autumn but became more abundant and spread to nearby sections of the cellar in Spring and Summer (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes temporal changes in C. santamariae distribution observed in the spatial mapping data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Micrococcus and Kocuria spread around floors and other surfaces in cellar, barrel room, and packaging areas.
source: Other taxa demonstrated more localized patterns of dispersion, such as Micrococcus and Kocuria, which appeared to spread the most around floors and other surfaces in cellar, barrel room, and packaging areas (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes spatial distribution patterns observed in Figure 6.

claim: Regular contact with beer runoff diluted with rinse water may support growth of Micrococcus and Kocuria populations.
source: Here, regular contact with beer runoff diluted with rinse water may support growth of these populations, which are associated with spoilage in low-alcohol beers (Back, 1981).
evidence: This is an inference about conditions supporting microbial growth, with a citation supporting the association with beer spoilage.

claim: Micrococcus and Kocuria are associated with spoilage in low-alcohol beers.
source: Here, regular contact with beer runoff diluted with rinse water may support growth of these populations, which are associated with spoilage in low-alcohol beers (Back, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Back, 1981.

claim: High populations of Acetobacter and Lactobacillus were found in areas where high volumes of wort and beer may be encountered.
source: High populations of Acetobacter and Lactobacillus were found more disparately, and specifically in areas where high volumes of wort and beer may be encountered: on conveyor belts and floors below packaging areas, hotside and cellar area sinks, and on sample ports for isolated fermenters and kegs (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of these bacteria observed in Figure 6.

claim: Physical barriers (e.g., walls) and physiochemical conditions (e.g., humidity and temperature control) can staunch the spread of some microbes.
source: Microbial confinement within discrete zones suggests that physical barriers (e.g., walls) and physiochemical conditions (e.g., humidity and temperature control) can staunch the spread of some microbes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns of microbial confinement.

claim: Non-production surfaces that encounter beer and/or waste streams are typically only cleaned by hose and may accumulate substrates for supporting microbial growth and survival.
source: Non-production surfaces that encounter beer and/or waste streams, such as floors, sinks, and grain-handling equipment, are typically only cleaned by hose and may accumulate substrates for supporting microbial growth and survival.
evidence: This is an inference about cleaning practices and their effects on microbial growth.

claim: Aerosols and splashing occur regularly in a production brewery, increasing the likelihood for microbial spread and colonization.
source: Aerosols and splashing occur regularly in a production brewery (indeed, hosing down floors is one obvious cause), increasing the likelihood for microbial spread and colonization from these surfaces onto other surfaces, including equipment.
evidence: This is an inference about mechanisms of microbial dispersal in the brewery.

claim: Human and insect traffic can increase the rate of dispersal between surfaces.
source: Human and insect traffic can also increase the rate of dispersal between these surfaces (e.g., from one room to another).
evidence: This is an inference about potential vectors for microbial dispersal.

claim: Physical partitions appear to inhibit microbial passage between areas.
source: Physical partitions appear to inhibit this passage as observed in this brewery and, where possible, may reduce the probability for contamination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns of microbial distribution.

claim: Separating packaging rooms from cellar and hotside operations may help protect packaging surfaces and beer from contamination.
source: Separating packaging rooms from cellar and hotside operations and using local partitions, such as blast shields, may help protect packaging surfaces and beer from such routes of contamination.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed patterns of microbial dispersal.

claim: The brewery studied rarely suffers from any cases of product contamination.
source: These findings are instructive but indeed should not be interpreted with alarm: they illustrate microbial dispersal in a functioning brewery that rarely suffers from any cases of product contamination.
evidence: This provides context about the practical significance of the findings.

claim: Short 16S rRNA gene amplicons are frequently inadequate to resolve reliable species-level identifications.
source: However, short 16S rRNA gene amplicons are frequently inadequate to resolve reliable species-level identifications (Bokulich and Mills, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bokulich and Mills, 2012a.

claim: Different surface and sample types exhibit distinct lactic acid bacterial patterns, corresponding to the substrates encountered at that site or contained in that sample.
source: Results indicate that different surface and sample types exhibit distinct lactic acid bacterial patterns, corresponding to the substrates encountered at that site or contained in that sample (Figure 8).
evidence: This describes the results of the LAB-TRFLP analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Wort samples contained a mixture of Lactobacillus delbrueckii, Lactobacillus sakei, Lactobacillus hilgardii, Leuconostoc mesenteroides, Lactococcus lactis, Streptococcus sp., and Bacillus sp. A.
source: Wort samples contained a mixture of Lactobacillus delbrueckii, Lactobacillus sakei, Lactobacillus hilgardii, Leuconostoc mesenteroides, Lactococcus lactis, Streptococcus sp., and Bacillus sp. A, most of which were only rarely detected in other fermenting and bottled beer samples.
evidence: This describes the LAB community composition in wort samples.

claim: Many LAB species detected in wort are rarely found in beers.
source: Many of these species are also rarely found in beers (Bokulich and Bamforth, 2013), but instead appear associated with grain, hence their detection in wort.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and inference about the source of these LAB.

claim: Coolship and fermenting sour beers were dominated by Pediococcus and/or L. lindneri.
source: Coolship and fermenting sour beers (in this case coolship beers produced from different wort types) were dominated by Pediococcus and/or L. lindneri, corroborating previous studies of coolship beers in this brewery (Bokulich et al., 2012b).
evidence: This describes the LAB community composition in coolship beers and is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fermenters and barrel surfaces that contacted coolship fermentations exhibited similar LAB communities to the beers, though Lactobacillus brevis and Lactobacillus sp. A were more common on these surfaces.
source: Fermenters and barrel surfaces that contacted these fermentations near the time of sampling exhibited similar communities, though Lactobacillus brevis and Lactobacillus sp. A were more common on these surfaces than in the beers or on other surfaces.
evidence: This describes the LAB community composition on surfaces contacting coolship beers.

claim: Floor and packaging area surfaces contained a diverse mixture of LAB, primarily L. lindneri, L. brevis, and L. delbrueckii.
source: Floor and packaging area surfaces contained a more diverse mixture of LAB, but primarily the L. lindneri, L. brevis, and L. delbrueckii detected in the wort and beer samples.
evidence: This describes the LAB community composition on floor and packaging surfaces.

claim: Only Pediococcus was detected on grain samples.
source: Interestingly, only Pediococcus was detected on grain samples, though only weak amplification could be had from these samples, suggesting low LAB populations or inhibition of PCR by grain polyphenols, possibly suppressing the detection of less abundant populations.
evidence: This describes the LAB detected on grain samples and provides possible explanations for limited detection.

claim: Hop pellet samples contained a mixture of different LAB populations, including Pediococcus, L. lindneri, and L. brevis.
source: Hop pellet samples also contained a mixture of different LAB populations, including Pediococcus, L. lindneri, and L. brevis.
evidence: This describes the LAB community composition in hop samples.

claim: Substrate drives the composition of LAB communities as well as whole microbial communities.
source: These results illustrate that substrate drives the composition of LAB communities as well as whole microbial communities and highlight the risk of cross-contamination between different equipment surfaces.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LAB-TRFLP results.

claim: Lactobacillus spp. were detected on both filler heads, including one used only for conventional beer packaging.
source: The detection of Lactobacillus spp. on both filler heads (only one of which is used for sour beer packaging) makes this observation all the more pertinent.
evidence: This describes a specific finding highlighting cross-contamination risk.

claim: Cross-contamination between processing areas is very likely the prevailing cause of spoilage in any brewery.
source: This observation is not likely to be an exceptional case; cross-contamination between processing areas is very likely the prevailing cause of spoilage in any brewery, where microbial biofilms have been previously reported even on packaging equipment (Timke et al., 2005; Storgards et al., 2006; Timke et al., 2008; Mamvura et al., 2011; Matoulkova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies on biofilms in breweries.

claim: Beer-spoiling LAB possess several mechanisms that support their growth and survival in beer.
source: Beer-spoiling LAB possess several mechanisms that support their growth and survival in beer (Suzuki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2006.

claim: Hop-resistance genes including horA, horB, horC, and hitA are upregulated during growth in beer.
source: Hop-resistant LAB typically contain several of these genes, including horA (Sami et al., 1997; Sakamoto et al., 2001), horB (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), horC (Suzuki et al., 2005; Iijima et al., 2006), and hitA (Hayashi et al., 2001), which are upregulated during growth in beer (Bergsveinson et al., 2012; Pittet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The presence of hop-resistance genes within brewery environments and on brewing equipment has not been described previously.
source: However, the presence of these genes within brewery environments and on brewing equipment has not been described previously.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the study's investigation of hop-resistance genes in brewery environments.

claim: Sour beer samples contained the highest counts of horC, between 2.0 × 10^4–4.8 × 10^4 copies/µl.
source: Results demonstrate high gene frequencies on several surfaces within the brewery (Figure 9). Sour beer samples contained the highest counts, between 2.0 × 104–4.8 × 104 copies/µl of horC, but fermenter and packaging area surfaces (filler heads, below bottling line belt, and packaging sink) also registered between 2.8–7.8 × 102 copies/cm2.
evidence: This reports quantitative results from the ddPCR analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Fermenter and packaging area surfaces registered between 2.8–7.8 × 10^2 copies/cm^2 of hop-resistance genes.
source: Results demonstrate high gene frequencies on several surfaces within the brewery (Figure 9). Sour beer samples contained the highest counts, between 2.0 × 104–4.8 × 104 copies/µl of horC, but fermenter and packaging area surfaces (filler heads, below bottling line belt, and packaging sink) also registered between 2.8–7.8 × 102 copies/cm2.
evidence: This reports quantitative results from the ddPCR analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: No hop-resistance alleles were detected on hop samples, keg samples, or one barrel bung sample.
source: None of these alleles were detected on hop samples, keg samples, or one barrel bung (stopper) sample, though 1.1 × 103 total copies/cm2 were detected on a keg faucet used for attaching kegs to beer lines at the brewery.
evidence: This reports negative and positive detection results from the ddPCR analysis.
